We tackle challenges like navigating lengthy development cycles, regulatory hurdles, and ethical questions in defense tech and plus Jake offers advice on DoD procurement, the value of defense for strategies, and leveraging public engagement for sector awareness. Finally we explore the role of strategic partnerships and the future of a more diverse group of buyers for M &A in the defense tech markets. One of the great things about the Venice Biennale is it's not just the Giardini or the Arsenale where art is staged. In fact, like the water on which Venice floats, the entire city is seeped with art. And what I want to do is to explore the various far -flung pavilions that have been colonised by artists this year. Here in St Mark's Square at the illustrious Musée Carrère is an exhibition by the British sculptor Sir Anthony Caro. It's a beautifully judged show from the artists who quite literally as well as metaphorically knocked sculpture off the pedestal and onto the floor and into our space. And who produced radical painted abstract steel sculptures at the beginning of the 60s that the American critic Clement Greenberg said were revolutionary. And midway between St Mark's Square and the Rialto, this elegant palazzo, the Pisani, has been turned into a Scottish pavilion. There are three artists on show. Corinne Swann uses work that her father did in the early 70s as a social anthropologist in Peru. Duncan Campbell reworks a forgotten film, The Statues Also Die by Chris Marker and Alan René. And Hayley Tompkins has a series of found images, photographs, which she shows on the floor but seems to abstract a particular colour or hue to make us look again intently and in slightly different ways. And in this vine -covered courtyard, just off the main drag, a newcomer to the Biennale, Hong Kong. This is interesting. A guard box, something you might find outside a factory, with the window smeared with some substance that, I swear, I get a niff of Nivea. Now inside, more conventional artistic references, paintings, beautifully productively produced, a table with the signs of some kind of activity, creative or otherwise, a vacuum cleaner, a t -shirt. This work by Lee Kidd is a single installation made up of a whole series of individual pieces. But actually, it seems somehow to be a piece about where art ends and life begins. It's a kind of dystopian non -place, but at the same time seems extraordinarily familiar too. Basically, think we're in limbo land.

Why does Britain look the way it does? Why are some regions mountainous, others flat, some fertile, others difficult to farm? Because the shape of the land is not accidental. It's the result of forces that have been acting for millions of years. Welcome to the making of Britain. Britain's landscape can feel familiar, even predictable. Hills, valleys, plains and coastlines form a pattern that seems settled and permanent. But beneath that familiarity lies a complex geological history. The land has been folded, uplifted, eroded and reshaped over vast periods of time. Mountain ranges formed and wore down. Rivers carved their paths. Glaciers moved across the surface, altering everything in their path. The result is a landscape that reflects layers of change, each stage leaving its mark on what exists today. One of the most noticeable features of Britain is the contrast between different regions. The north and west tend to be higher, more rugged, more resistant to change. The south and east are generally lower, flatter and more suited to agriculture. This pattern is not random. It reflects the underlying geology. It Older, harder rocks in the north and west. younger, softer rocks in the south and east. Features such as pennines act as natural divides, influencing movement, settlement and communication. These divisions have shaped not just the physical landscape, but the human one as well. Water has played a central role in shaping the land. Rivers have cut through rock, creating valleys that provide routes for travel and settlement. These valleys often became the sites of towns and cities, offering access to water, fertile land and transport. Over time, river systems helped define regions, linking some areas while separating others. The courses of rivers were not designed with human use in mind, but they became integral to it. They influenced where people lived, how they moved and how communities developed. The last ice age left a profound imprint on Britain. Glaciers covered large parts of the land, grinding down surfaces, carving out valleys and depositing material as they advanced and retreated. When the ice melted, it left behind a landscape that had been fundamentally altered. Hills were reshaped, valleys deepened and new features created. The effects of this period are still visible today, from the shape of the countryside to the distribution of soils. The land that emerged was not the same as the land that had existed before. At this point, it's worth considering how much of what we see as natural or inevitable is actually the result of long processes of change. When looking at the landscape, does it appear fixed or does it suggest a history of transformation? But how much do you think these physical features still influence where people live and how they move today? Share your thoughts in the comments, because the relationship between land and life is central to this story. The shape of the land has always influenced how it is used. In flatter, more fertile areas, agriculture could be developed more easily, supporting larger populations. In more rugged regions, farming was more difficult, often limited to grazing rather than crop production. This created patterns of settlement that reflected the capabilities of the land. Dense populations developed in some areas, while others remained sparsely inhabited. These patterns were not simply the result of choice. They were shaped by what the land could support. Geography can act as both a barrier and a route. Mountain ranges, hills and difficult terrain can limit movement, creating division between regions. At the same time, valleys, plains and coastlines can facilitate connection. In Britain, these features have played a role in shaping communication and interaction. Some areas became centres of exchange and movement, while others remained more isolated. Over time, these differences contributed to regional identities, influenced by both proximity and separation. From a modern perspective, with advanced transport and infrastructure, the limitations imposed by geography may seem less significant. But for most of history, they were central. Travel was slower, more difficult and more dependent on the terrain. Settlements developed where conditions allowed. And routes followed the easiest paths through the landscape. The decisions people made were shaped by these realities. They built where it was practical, moved where it was possible and adapted to the conditions they faced. The shape of the land was not something to be overcome easily. It was something to be worked with. Over time, the physical characteristics of regions became part of how they were understood. The ruggedness of some areas, the openness of others, the fertility or difficulty of the land. These features contributed to local identities. They influenced ways of life, economic activities and cultural perceptions. While these associations are not fixed or universal, they reflect a long -standing connection between people and place. The land is not just a backdrop. It is part of the story. The shape of the land continues to influence Britain. The infrastructure follows routes determined by geography. Cities expand within the limits set by terrain. Agricultural patterns reflect the underlying condition of soil and the landscape. While technology has reduced some of these constraints, it has not removed them entirely. The imprint of geological processes remains visible, shaping decisions in ways that are sometimes obvious, sometimes subtle. I'm Rebecca Vincent, the Director of International Campaigns for Reporters Without Borders. I'm outside the Old Bailey Court in London at the end of the last day in four weeks of evidence in the US extradition proceedings against WikiLeaks publisher Julian Assange. Reporters Without Borders has been monitoring throughout these four weeks despite severe restrictions imposed on observers by the court. The judge refused to recognize or accommodate the role of professional NGO observers as being any different to the public. So the only way we've been able to follow this case has been to queue and to get support from grassroots activists who have also queued and held our place on many days to gain one of the very few spaces in the public gallery. This is not how we're accustomed to working, it's not how we monitor cases in other countries and it did not allow us to fully monitor in the way that we would have liked to. But what we did witness was alarming. We remain convinced that Mr. Assange has been targeted for his contributions to journalism. The evidence heard really strengthened that case. The fact that the Espionage Act has been applied in a political way. The fact that because the Espionage Act does not have a public interest offence, if Mr. Assange faces prosecution in the US he's unable to use that, which is a compelling argument, because the information that was published was in the public interest. We heard from a range of medical experts about Mr. Assange's physical health, his mental health, and in that regard we have concerns from a humanitarian perspective as well. Mr. Assange suffers from depression, has frequent suicidal thoughts, experiences auditory hallucinations, has suffered PTSD, has a sleeping disorder, among other issues, all which make him extremely vulnerable. Several experts testified that if he is forced to endure the conditions that he would face being held in the United States, that he would be very likely to attempt suicide. So in some ways his extradition is a matter of possible life or death. We continue to call for Mr. Assange's unconditional release. We believe that the charges against him should be dropped, that he should not spend another night in prison. He should not have been there in the first place, and he certainly should not be extradited to the United States. We will continue to follow proceedings and do our jobs to the best of our abilities, but we'll be calling again on the court to reconsider its position with regard to NGO observers, and we'll be seeking to escalate that complaint in other ways as well, because we feel that this is not in accordance with the UK's obligations to the principles of open justice and the right to a fair trial. And it's not just those rights that are at stake here, it's the public's right to information. The public has a right to know what's happened here at the Old Bailey the past four weeks. The public had a right to the stories that came out as a result of the publication of leaked information. So it's not just a question of Mr. Assange's rights or our ability as NGO observers to monitor, but of the public's right to information, because that's what is at stake ultimately in this case. It is the future of journalism, the future of press freedom, not only in the US or the UK, but internationally. What these governments are doing is a political persecution intended to set a dangerous precedent for journalism, and that must be acknowledged as such. We will continue to raise concern where we can at RSF and to stick with this case. are also trying terms Answers We you.
sources.title: 4 weeks of evidence in the US extradition case against Wikileaks publisher Julian Assange

The state's training manuals and operating manuals for the speed measuring device. 5. The officer's log book of tickets written on the day of defendant's alleged violation. 6. The repair history of the speed measuring device used to determine defendant's speed for the past 12 months. 7. Any engineering and speed studies used to set the speed limit at the section of highway where defendant's speed was measured. 7. The appellate court also found that the stalker LADAR speed measuring device had not been proven to be scientifically reliable, and as such, the results of its operation should not have been admitted during the municipal court proceedings or considered by the law division. 8. The court remanded the matter to the law division for a plenary hearing on the scientific reliability of the stalker LADAR. 8. it is determined to be reliable, then the matter is remanded to the municipal court for trial after the state has provided all the discovery required by this opinion. 8. Sandwiched in between the magnitude and visibility of World War II and the heartbreak and scorn of the Vietnam War is the Korean War. Nearly 1.8 million Americans served in Korea during the three years that made up the shooting war. More than 33,000 lost their lives in battle. The exact number of Iowans who fought in Korea is unknown, but 508 made the ultimate sacrifice. Many of those who fought in Korea came home and melted back into society. Little is devoted to the war in most public school history texts, but for most veterans, the experience remains a turning point in their lives. The American Public Television. forces fell back as the invading army swept towards the southern tip of the peninsula. Combat is not a pleasant experience. And you're scared. And if somebody tells you they're not scared in combat, they're lying. You're thinking about saving your life and saving the lives of your buddy next to you and your other buddies also. If you weren't religious when you get in combat, you'll get religious in a hurry. When somebody's shooting at you and people are dying around you from gunshot wounds or artillery or motor rounds, you soon get religion in a hurry. And you pray a lot. A lot of guys claim that they didn't. Well, I can tell you that they did because it scares the living Jesus out of you. Or I should say it scares the Jesus living in you.

[SPEAKER_03]
In order to deal with the job they had to do on the battlefield, many soldiers used racial epithets to dehumanize the people they were fighting. While these terms are no longer acceptable, it was what was done by many who fought in Korea.

[SPEAKER_07]
We called them gooks. The enemy, the Orientals, we called them gooks. And we looked down upon them, which maybe we shouldn't have done religiously, but they were human beings. But that was our objective was to kill the gooks, as we called it. And that was your objective, so that's what we did. And sometimes it would get pretty personal.

[SPEAKER_03]
Gates moved from place to place like most troops on the ground, on his feet.

[SPEAKER_07]
We were exhausted because we were on the move constantly. Constantly. And then it would be, well, do you think they can find it so we can get something to eat? Sometimes they wouldn't find us for a couple days, because we'd be on the move. They hired over 300,000 South Korean kids. They're little bitty guys. They hauled everything on their backs, our sea rations, whatever we needed. Ammunitions came to us on the backs of South Korean kids. Because there was no interstructure in the country for heavy truck traffic to get supplies up. Yeah, you can do air drops, but you still have to have somebody get the stuff and bring it up to the line to you. Over 3,000 of those kids died doing that during the Korean War because the North Koreans and Chinese knew what they were doing. And so if they got a chance to pick them off, they would.

[SPEAKER_03]
By March of 1952, Gates had enough points to go home.

[SPEAKER_07]
When I came back in the rotation, the Korean War was still going on over there. I came from San Diego to Des Moines on the train.

[SPEAKER_03]
When he arrived at the train station in Des Moines, he decided to take a cab the four blocks to his parents' house.

[SPEAKER_07]
I was in my Marine uniform and I had my ribbons on. He helped me get my sea bag in there. I told him where I wanted to go and he knew and I got there, he wouldn't take any money. He said, thank you for your service. I owe this to you. I'm not taking your money. So he wouldn't charge me for taking me to my folks' house, which I thanked him for doing that. I guess my biggest fear was I was going to have to go back if they couldn't get it settled.

[SPEAKER_03]
Elmer Hassanmiller, Jr., from Grand Mound, had been called to serve near the end of World War II, but was given a deferment just before the war ended. When the Korean War broke out, he was immediately drafted into the Army. Hassanmiller received training as an artilleryman and forward observer and was shipped to Korea in May of 1951.

[None]
My

[SPEAKER_10]
first night on the front lines, I was artillery support for the Turkish United Nation troops. And the first night the North Koreans hit and they got so close to overrunning us, they were throwing grenades on the hill with us before we beat them off. So we just had to fight them off by hand or with our

[None]
side arms

[SPEAKER_10]
and so on.

[SPEAKER_03]
From his observation post, he could see Hill 931, which became important real estate in the tough battles of Heartbreak Ridge and Bloody Ridge. One day, Hassanmiller was sitting with his buddy, Henry Turk, from Texas, watching F -86 Sabre jets drop napalm on Hill 931. A small plane was spotting targets for the faster jets.

[None]
One

[SPEAKER_10]
of the guys said to the spotter plane, I have troops in the open. And the spotter plane guy said, go ahead. Well, the jets turned around and here they come directly at us where we were. And we kept looking and looking and all of a sudden one of them started smoking. And I said, there a machine gun? And I drove in a trench and Henry Turk, he landed on top of me and they machine gunned us. And

[None]
I grabbed

[SPEAKER_10]
the radio and I used a few harsh words to tell them if that's all the better you can do, you just machine gun your own troops. Go back to Japan, wherever you came from and stay there. And they turned around and made their second run. Only this time, they knew where we were at. They went right over us and they dropped two more bombs on 931. And when they come to turn around this time, they come and go home. They were more than eight feet above us. The draft from them two planes was something

[None]
different.

[SPEAKER_10]
Never heard a thing about it.

[SPEAKER_03]
His position was often a distance from the front line. But that didn't mean he could drop his guard.

[SPEAKER_10]
I was taking a new guy with me and we going along and all of a sudden a lot of fire and we dove off the trail. I had 30 round clips in my carbine and I emptied one of them out and part of another one and the thing got quiet. And I crawled up there while the air laid a North Korean and I thought he was dead. And I walked over on the other end of there, there were two old people sitting there. They were dead. And I heard something behind me and that North Korean was just picking up his gun. And I cut loose with my carbine and I had three shells in that last clip. And I hit all three in his head. You know what that does to your head? Just in the grates. He's dead now.

[SPEAKER_03]
Hassan Miller was in Korea for 10 and a half months before earning enough points to go home.

[SPEAKER_10]
Well, I was working the day they called me down there at one o 'clock one afternoon. They said, get your ass down here and go on home. You didn't have to say it twice. So I went down there and thought there was a bunch more. Something that were going some direction too. And so that night there was a hell of a party.

[SPEAKER_03]
Eventually, Hassan Miller made it back to Iowa.

[SPEAKER_10]
One thing we were looked down on, only one guy greeted me. Well, Vietnam's a little that way too. After 10 and a half months of that, Dwight. Well, I think of Korea every day.

[None]
Can't forget

[SPEAKER_10]
it. I think a lot of people are afraid to ask about it. I've been a Legion member for 66 years. And I have a big turkey supper once a year for Thanksgiving. And there's some Vietnam veterans. And I made some comments sitting beside the one guy about fighting in Korea. And he asked me a couple of questions. Well, then there were a couple of guys across the table. They were interested too. Boy, they started asking questions about the fighting and all that stuff. They were really interested. most generally, a lot of people, they didn't give a damn.

[SPEAKER_03]
Don Stuva from rural Fontenelle was drafted into the Army in 1951. By August, he was among the replacement infantrymen sent to Korea. After a few days in Seoul, he was deployed north.

[SPEAKER_08]
We were up at midnight and the chaplain of the outfit gathered us all together. And of course, he prayed for us. And I can still see him and remember the words that he spoke. He said, some of you are going to live, some of you are going to die. And he never pulled any punches. And then I can't recall, but it seems to me like we started walking from there into the battle zone. And that was at midnight. And then right at dawn, just as it was breaking dawn, we arrived in the battle zone. And we were the second wave to go in. That was when I really woke up to reality because they were carrying the dead and the wounded out as we were coming in. Anyway, it was a man that was on a stretcher. You could still see his face, the pain and the, and the, I don't know how you can describe it. But he'd been hit in the stomach and his whole stomach was tore open and I could see his insides. And he was still alive. And that's when I realized that this is real. I really had no ill will like a lot of people had hate for their enemy, but I never hated them. My thoughts were that probably those soldiers didn't want to be there any more

[None]
than I did.

[SPEAKER_08]
I never had any feeling that I was going to die, even though I recognized the fact that that was a possibility. I went in there with my belief in the Lord. I knew in my heart that God could save me or deliver me or protect me, but I wasn't sure that he would.

[SPEAKER_03]
His belief was reinforced one night during a battle on a mountain top.

[SPEAKER_08]
I was laying there one time and, and on my stomach, trying and crawling and the bullets come by, just kicking up dirt in my face. I can remember that. And that's so many times. And that's just like that, that did so many close that, I never got hit when so many other people around me did. And so I can only say that it was a miraculous thing that God had protected me.

[SPEAKER_03]
Korea was the first war where African Americans and whites battled the enemy side by side in large numbers. Previous to the Korean War, a general mixing of races had been the exception and not the rule.

[SPEAKER_08]
Most of the time that I was in Korea was with, uh, that I was in the foxhole was with a colored partner. That didn't make any difference to me. I didn't have any, anything against anybody.

[SPEAKER_03]
Stuva made a few friends in combat and lost a few the same way. One of them was mortally wounded during a nighttime patrol.

[SPEAKER_08]
He stepped on a mine and it blew both of his legs basically off. That was about eight o 'clock at night when it was just before dark. And then he laid there all night. I stayed with him. And so it was eight or nine o 'clock in the next morning when the killer had come in to take him out. And, uh, but he lived all that time until just the time the helicopter was coming and he died. That's when you realize that war is hell and why. My thoughts were always this, this. If the people that caused these wars, if they had to still, they'd be on line and do the fighting, there wouldn't be any war. But then that's not the way it is.

[SPEAKER_03]
George Sam Buck was sent to Korea in March of 1953. The young man from Lineville had transferred from the Air Force to the Army so he could attend Officer Candidate School or OCS.

[SPEAKER_06]
You know, in fact, the OCS class ahead of me all went to Germany. And I was hoping that I could go to Germany rather than Korea, but, uh, I didn't.

[SPEAKER_03]
In March of 1953, the newly minted second lieutenant arrived in Korea and was sent 60 miles northeast of Seoul to outpost Harry in the Iron Triangle, a site of heavy fighting throughout the war. On June 10th, Buck was sent to observe enemy troops. As night fell, he made his way back to the command bunker to speak with Captain Martin Markley, his commanding officer, and Lieutenant George Richards, the executive officer. And all of a sudden,

[None]
the

[SPEAKER_06]
shells just came all over us, you know. The exec officer, he said, uh, they're in the trenches. And, uh, that's about the last words he said.

[SPEAKER_03]
Chinese forces stormed up the hill and trapped the soldiers in the command bunker. Markley and Richards began firing over Buck's head. Buck got on the radio to call for artillery support. At one point, he called in fire directly on their position. That took a

[None]
little... a

[SPEAKER_06]
little something that I had never thought of, you know, as plain

[None]
suicide. Before

[SPEAKER_03]
the battle began, Markley, Richards, and Buck had set grenades outside the bunker door. The plan had been to throw the grenades onto attacking troops. The plan backfired. Attacking Chinese soldiers used the grenades against the trapped men.

[SPEAKER_06]
And they would throw in the grenade, and then they'd try to run in behind it. And for some reason, I don't know why, but I would step around and catch them as they started in. And, uh, and then they'd throw a grenade, and I'd duck back.

[SPEAKER_03]
As the Chinese soldiers came through the door, Buck shot each one with his.30 caliber carbine.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_06]
it had a lever on it that you could push it forward, and it would fire automatically. And if it wasn't forward, it would fire. See why? Automatically. So I got, you know, pretty scared, and I pushed that lever forward. I wish I'd never done that, because I went through, uh, 130 -some rounds. And I thought, well, Abbey Nation. And that was a... was a problem.

[SPEAKER_03]
The Chinese troops kept throwing grenades at Buck until his luck ran out.

[None]
The

[SPEAKER_06]
grenade that got me, it got my right leg and right arm, and... And, well, just... just my whole right side, you know, I got hit by fragments.

[SPEAKER_03]
His right hand was badly injured, and he was unable to fire his carbine. Captain Markley was seriously wounded, and Richards was dead. Buck was now alone in the fight. Enemy soldiers began passing by the bunker and looking in the door.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_06]
I knew I was in trouble then, and I took this bloody hand and wiped it over my face, and I played dead. And when they came in, well, they looked at me, and it just... It felt like their flashlight was burning me, you know, that light of it was... And I thought, oh, God, I hope they can't... They

[None]
don't know

[SPEAKER_06]
I'm alive.

[SPEAKER_03]
Friendly forces arrived and took back the bunker. A medic came in, treated Buck's wounds, and the pair began to work on saving Captain Markley's life. The medic rolled the severely injured officer over onto Buck's lap.

[SPEAKER_06]
And his one eye was laying on his cheek, and the socket was full of dirt and stuff. And the medic started to work it on his head. And I didn't have nothing to do. So I saw that eyeball, so I cleaned the socket out, and I shoved that eyeball back in place. And believe it or not, he had it when he died.

[SPEAKER_03]
The medic left to treat other wounded soldiers. In desperation, Buck left the bunker twice more to find someone to help him take Markley down the hill.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_06]
I was crawling over dead bodies, Chinese and American young kids, you know, staring straight at the sky. And they shouldn't have ever been there. They just looked like high school kids. bodies.

[SPEAKER_03]
It took a year for his wounds to heal. Markley also went home for an extended convalescence and recovery. Buck received little or no recognition for his actions during the one critical night of heavy fighting. Captain Markley petitioned for a higher honor. Five decades after the bloody battle ended, Buck was awarded the Silver Star for conspicuous gallantry in action. Robbie Robinson from Waterloo was drafted into the Army after graduating from high school in 1952. By the spring of 1953, Robinson received orders for Korea.

[None]
He

[SPEAKER_04]
had a number, and you probably know your number now. My number's US 55309446. And that was my name. So every morning I look on my list on the board. I said, oh man, that's my damn name. I said, damn. I said, I better write my mom's here. I'm going over Korea.

[SPEAKER_03]
Peace talks were still going on when Robinson's ship departed for Korea.

[SPEAKER_04]
The guys in the bottom ship, you know, what you do, you're shooting dice and doing whatever. And every day, everybody got quiet to listen because they was hoping that they would negotiate peace, that we would, about time we got to Korea, we wouldn't have to. It didn't happen. Everybody got down. It was comical, but not comical. Everybody got religion, some of them.

[SPEAKER_03]
After arriving in Korea, Robinson was sent to a replacement depot. He remembers falling into formation every morning and seeing trucks returning from the front, filled with soldiers.

[SPEAKER_04]
Whoever was head of the compound. And the truckers were bringing these people off the line going home, wounded or going home. And he would ask the trucker, how many you got on there? He would say, oh, we got eight. How many? So that trucker was from a second division or maybe 40th division or, you know, whatever. So, okay, you, you, you, you, take one step forward. Get on that truck. You're in the second division. And so you talking about some bitching. Well, I'm not an infantryman. Oh, yes, you are. I'm gonna write my signature. I'm gonna write all that book. That didn't mean nothing.

[SPEAKER_03]
When it came to who stood beside you in combat, Robinson echoed the views of other soldiers who had come before him. It made no difference what color you were as long as you backed up the other soldiers in your unit.

[SPEAKER_04]
They used to razz me because I'm Iowa, black boy in Iowa. What are you doing, Iowa? You farm? I'll go to hell. You get what I'm saying? He and I do that. was telling me I'm brand new. All you do is whatever that sergeant tell you you do.

[SPEAKER_03]
Nightly patrols had gone from conquest and capture to just observation.

[SPEAKER_04]
It wasn't like maybe a year or two before I got there. All these bands' eyes and all this kind of stuff. He had to quiet it down quite a bit. We had a lot of artillery firing back and forth at each other. And you could see them way over the hill and they could see us. But let's patrol at night. That was the one I would worry about because it's dark. We could hear them, but we couldn't tell exactly where the fire was coming from, when they would shoot. And boy, when they would shoot, everybody hit the ground, you know. We had a radio man. We would call back up to the front line, our line. And no contact, and we're coming back in. When we come back across the line, do not shoot us. You know what I'm saying? We're the friendly troops. And then we come back. And then next night, maybe somebody else be chosen. I'm young and dumb. Wasn't scared a bit.

[SPEAKER_03]
As July 1953 dawned, it appeared some kind of deal was close at hand.

[SPEAKER_04]
We knew it was getting close. Every night we would listen. Probably one guy or two would have a radio in the whole damn company. So you were arguing and fighting with him because he wanted to hear country music. I want to hear jazz. But anyway, when that came on about the ceasefire, it was big news. It was right now we knew it. And then at the end, on 27th of July 1953 when it stopped, boy, we shot up like 4th of July. We was on the hill cause. did not want to bring, had to carry all of them down, ammo down the hill. And we just, I mean, we were blowing up. And that was a great day. The war, you know, they stopped. But as I look back at my time, said, boy, I was lucky. 20 years old, 19 years old. In Korea? What in the hell is Korea, you know? And I think it's very smart what they do. They get the youngest kid. Wasn't scared of nothing, you see. Hoping I can see something so I can be a bad man with my gun, you know. Not knowing that, hell, I might get hit. But that wasn't in my mind.

[SPEAKER_03]
The fighting had lasted three years, one month, and three days. Technically, both countries are still at war. With few exceptions, the ceasefire has endured for 70 years. As they came home, some of the soldiers brought wounds that they kept hidden. Dennis Dorman clearly remembers the day the ceasefire was signed. He was still drinking to blot out the memories of combat.

[SPEAKER_05]
Dennis stayed drunk for a lot of years. Went through a couple of wives. And then my third wife said one day, she said, something's got to go with you or the booze. And for the first time in my life, I thought more of someone than I did of something. And I said, I'll quit. And I had to go to jail that weekend before I finally got my act together. And I've been sober 47 years now. I've had people say, well, you're a hero. And I tell them, the heroes are still there. I'm here.

[SPEAKER_03]
They're my heroes. Bill Harrison had difficulty sleeping when he returned.

[SPEAKER_09]
Most nights I have nightmares, I remember. Only sometimes in my dreams I see a lot more detail than I realized I did then. I was finally diagnosed with what they called post -combat stress then. But I got past that. Once I knew what it was, I could deal with it. I never even told my wife anything.

[SPEAKER_03]
Don Stuva spent years wondering if his service in Korea was worth it.

[SPEAKER_08]
I've often thought to myself, I would never ever want to go through that again or wish anybody else to go through it. yet the experience there, I realize what it is by far more than I would if I'd never went through it. And so that's the only good thing I can see about it. You know, I can share that war is hell. And that's what basically, yeah, we avoid it if it's all possible. But I didn't really believe in it because I thought, what good is it? You know, what are we doing here? Why are we fighting? It wasn't until years later when I began to realize the importance of fighting for freedom.

[None]
You know so,

[SPEAKER_01]

The Republican senator represented Southwest Virginia in the 38th district since 2014. Chafin first served in the Virginia House of Delegates in 2013. Senate Republicans and Governor Ralph Northam both issued statements of sympathy to the senator's family, both saying Southwest Virginia has lost a fierce advocate. And then, you know, bringing some of those companies in as DARPA performers outside of the traditional pool that I just described a minute ago, you know, and saying, okay, you've got some limits but if you took this program manager's big idea and you were able to push it, what could you do, right? And so making that marriage happen, it's happened in places within DARPA, but as an organization trying to find a way to better link the two communities is really what we're after. Awesome. Clay?

[SPEAKER_01]
We okay? Where's my answer?

You can, if you've got an idea of a way to solve a DOD problem, you can reach out to me on LinkedIn. If you're a venture partner, if you're a VC, we've got a mailing list and we will literally send you our list of stuff that we're interested in. The second way is we have routine events. So, is anybody familiar with GIFICS? Very few. Okay. So, you can Google GIFICS. It's run by the Naval Post Graduate School. But that's an example of a capability where we have where you can bring your technology out for free and let DOD warfighters play with it and tell you, no, the button needs to go over here or go over there. And that's a hands -on experience. then the third thing we have, which we also run through SAM.gov, is our innovation outreach program, which is one where we leverage the venture community a lot. Because if you're a venture capital firm on our email list, every time we run a problem through innovation outreach, we'll send it to you. And the ask is very low barrier. [SPEAKER_02]

[None]
you know, it's like,

[SPEAKER_00]
so it's like, do we believe that competition will drive productivity? I do. And so the consolidation, it was like we lost it then in a sense.

[SPEAKER_01]

[SPEAKER_02]

[None]

So when we were building submarine -launched ballistic missiles, we had four competing programs. We had fundamental uncertainty. Should it be solid fuel? Should it be liquid fuel? The Investor With Joel Palathinkal
The Investor with Joel Palathinkal is a global omni channel show which highlights institutional investors from all walks of life and supports the continuing education for the next generation of allocators

S1 E96 • Jun 29, 2025 • 42 mins
In this episode, Jake Chapman from Marquee Ventures shares his journey into venture capital, emphasizing his defense-focused strategy and the founding of Marquee Ventures. He explores opportunities within defense technology sectors and the transformative role of AI in modern warfare. Jake offers insights into best practices for due diligence in defense investments and essential skills for venture fund managers. The discussion highlights managing venture funds, supporting portfolio companies, and building strong team cultures. Jake also shares effective networking and relationship-building strategies, investing strategies for hard tech companies, and concludes with valuable advice for investors and entrepreneurs.
Key Points
The US Department of Defense has historically played a significant role in seeding companies that have created groundbreaking technologies like the internet, GPS, and touchscreen interfaces.
Marquee Ventures focuses on deep tech sectors such as energy, applied AI, autonomy, and synthetic biology, recognizing their potential for defense applications and the importance of bridging the gap between innovative founders and government contracts.
The advancement of AI, especially in areas like deepfake detection and automated compliance, presents both significant opportunities and challenges for national security, with the potential to revolutionize processes from battlefield assessments to regulatory compliance.

E60 – GPS-Free Navigation
How do systems operate when GPS disappears?
Mike sits down with Kara Kramer, Vice President ofRaptor Sales at Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), to discuss one of the most important challenges facing modern autonomous systems: operating when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or completely unavailable.
We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS
BONUS: Kara also shares her professional journey and how she got into the defense industry!
Whether you're building autonomous systems, working indefense technology, or simply interested in where drone technology is headed, this episode provides an inside look at one of the fastest-moving areas in aerospace.

E55 – Christine Fox: the REAL Charlie
There is a strange set of organizations that live betweenindustry and government called Federally Funded Research and Development Centers (FFRDCs) and University Affiliated Research Centers (UARCs).
They play an important—but largely misunderstood role—in national security.
What better way to understand it all than with a guest who’sone of the most famous pop-culture examples: Christine Fox.
She was the real person who was portrayed as ‘Charlie’,Maverick’s civilian love interest, in Top Gun! She spent 40+ years working as an analyst in UARCs and a civilian leader at the Pentagon, culminating in serving as the acting Deputy Secretary of Defense.
Today, she continues to serve as a Fellow at Johns HopkinsUniversity’s Applied Physics Lab (JHU APL), which is the nation’s largest UARC.
This interview has a ton of inside baseball that you won’t find anywhere else!

Test is where new military hardware goes to wait.
Mike sits down with Jenn Wilson, Head of Federal at Nominal, to talk about test and evaluation, the least glamorous gate between a program and the warfighter.
Nominal builds test data infrastructure for hardware. Founded in 2022 by Anduril, Palantir, and Lockheed Martin alumni, it reached a $1 billion valuation in March.
Jenn’s take is that acceleration comes from optimizing what you test for. Cutting test points is the wrong lever.

Test and evaluation as a mission enabler
High rate, multimodal test data
Real-time telemetry and closing the test loop
DARPA CIPHER Forge and digital twins
Closing the sim to real gap

E60 – GPS-Free Navigation
How do systems operate when GPS disappears?
Mike sits down with Kara Kramer, Vice President ofRaptor Sales at Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), to discuss one of the most important challenges facing modern autonomous systems: operating when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or completely unavailable.
We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS
BONUS: Kara also shares her professional journey and how she got into the defense industry!
Whether you're building autonomous systems, working indefense technology, or simply interested in where drone technology is headed, this episode provides an inside look at one of the fastest-moving areas in aerospace.

E59 – Business Breakdown: Anduril
Anduril Industries raised $5 billion at a reported $61billion valuation—putting a nine-year-old defense tech company in the same conversation as legacy primes that have been building weapons for generations.
How did they do it, what is their strategy, and does the math make sense?
In this episode, Mike and Matthew take a deep dive inside Anduril’s products, revenue, contracts, and business strategy. They break down the Series H raise, the company’s rapid valuation climb, the difference between contract ceilings and booked revenue, and why visible federal obligations onlytell part of the story.
They also examine Anduril’s expanding product portfolio, anddebate the core question behind the company’s $61B price tag: Is Anduril the future of defense industrial production, or is the market pricing in near-flawless execution?
Topics include:
- Anduril’s $5B Series H and $61B valuation
- The gap between reported revenue and visible federalobligations
- Why Special Operations and the Border Patrol matter morethan most people realize
- The $20B Army enterprise vehicle—and why it is a rail, not acheck
- Barracuda, Fury, Arsenal-1, and hyperscale defensemanufacturing
- How Anduril compares to Lockheed, Northrop, GeneralDynamics, RTX, and Palantir
- The bull and bear case for Anduril’s long-term strategy
- What to watch next: IPO timing, task orders, deliveries, andrevenue growth
- The real bet: for Anduril to justify today’s valuation, ithas to grow from a $2B revenue company into a $20B+ revenue company very quickly.

E56 – The Fury Origin Story
This is the untold origin story of the Fury CollaborativeCombat Aircraft (CCA), as told by those who lived it.
Scott Bledsoe and Joe Murray join Mike to talk about Fury’s very beginning—way back to 2016.
Now known as Anduril’s YFQ-44, Fury originated as an SBIR project from Blue Force Technologies and may go on to become a poster child of SBIR success stories. But it’s not all good news.
The experience—and the decision to sell to Anduril—motivated Scott and Joe to start a new type of investment fund called the DoD Accelerator.
DoD Accelerator bridges the gap between venture capital and private equity, addressing the ‘funding valley of death’ they faced and the factors that led to the decision to sell their company—and Fury—to Anduril.
This is packed with never-before-revealed details and serves as the backdrop for a broader conversation about the realities of having a company in the defense industry.

Mike and Jake host defense industry legend Norm Augustine in
a rare interview!
He started as an aeronautical engineer in the 1950s and rose
to become the first CEO of Lockheed Martin, before leaving it all.
He lived through the 1980s defense industry heyday, wrote a
hilarious book called ‘Augustine’s Laws ’ and led the industry through a massive consolidation in the early 1990s after the infamous ‘Last Supper.’ This is a first-hand account of how it all went down—he was in the room when it happened.

- President and Chairman of the Association of the United States Army
- Chairman of the National Academy of Engineering
- Served 16 years on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology
- traveled to 130 countries
- holds 34 honorary degrees
- received dozens of accolades, including the Pentagon’s highest civilian decoration, the Distinguished Civilian Service Award---FIVE TIMES.

Nominal builds test data infrastructure for hardware. Founded in 2022 by Anduril, Palantir, and Lockheed Martin alumni, it reached a $1 billion valuation in March.
Jenn’s take is that acceleration comes from optimizing what you test for. Cutting test points is the wrong lever.

High rate, multimodal test data
Real-time telemetry and closing the test loop
DARPA CIPHER Forge and digital twins

E60 – GPS-Free Navigation
How do systems operate when GPS disappears?
Mike sits down with Kara Kramer, Vice President ofRaptor Sales at Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), to discuss one of the most important challenges facing modern autonomous systems: operating when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or completely unavailable.
We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS
BONUS: Kara also shares her professional journey and how she got into the defense industry!
Whether you're building autonomous systems, working indefense technology, or simply interested in where drone technology is headed, this episode provides an inside look at one of the fastest-moving areas in aerospace.

E59 – Business Breakdown: Anduril
Anduril Industries raised $5 billion at a reported $61billion valuation—putting a nine-year-old defense tech company in the same conversation as legacy primes that have been building weapons for generations.
How did they do it, what is their strategy, and does the math make sense?
In this episode, Mike and Matthew take a deep dive inside Anduril’s products, revenue, contracts, and business strategy. They break down the Series H raise, the company’s rapid valuation climb, the difference between contract ceilings and booked revenue, and why visible federal obligations onlytell part of the story.
They also examine Anduril’s expanding product portfolio, anddebate the core question behind the company’s $61B price tag: Is Anduril the future of defense industrial production, or is the market pricing in near-flawless execution?
Topics include:
- Anduril’s $5B Series H and $61B valuation
- The gap between reported revenue and visible federalobligations
- Why Special Operations and the Border Patrol matter morethan most people realize
- The $20B Army enterprise vehicle—and why it is a rail, not acheck
- Barracuda, Fury, Arsenal-1, and hyperscale defensemanufacturing
- How Anduril compares to Lockheed, Northrop, GeneralDynamics, RTX, and Palantir
- The bull and bear case for Anduril’s long-term strategy
- What to watch next: IPO timing, task orders, deliveries, andrevenue growth
- The real bet: for Anduril to justify today’s valuation, ithas to grow from a $2B revenue company into a $20B+ revenue company very quickly.

Episode notes
Daniel Robbins interviews Jake Chapman about how Marque Ventures invests in early stage companies advancing U.S. national security and Western values. Jake shares how his work moved from private investing into rethinking venture activity inside the Department of War and back out again into building a private firm designed to fund the future of defense, dual use, and strategic technologies.
Key Discussion Points:
Jake explains that national security investing requires founders and investors to think like futurists and “skate to where the puck is going,” not just fund what is being used in today’s conflicts. He shares why the U.S. acquisition system is more predictable than many people assume, making defense spending and future capability needs easier to map than consumer behavior. He also breaks down why defense founders need someone on the team with direct military or procurement experience and why talking to the end user early is critical. The conversation expands into space, where Jake argues that space infrastructure is becoming economically and strategically essential, with the long term possibility of a true in space economy and even the need to defend assets beyond Earth.
Takeaways:
A major takeaway from the episode is that great defense founders are usually mission driven and deeply engaged with the real world problems they want to solve. Jake makes clear that VCs are not only evaluating the business, but the founder’s passion, thoughtfulness, and ability to answer hard questions under pressure. He also highlights that some of the biggest mistakes in pitching come from dismissing competitors, lacking energy, or building a product without understanding how the actual customer will use it. More broadly, the episode shows that national security innovation is no longer a government only game, but a rapidly evolving startup space where private builders, veterans, and frontier tech founders can shape the future.
Closing Thoughts:
This Founder’s Story episode captures just how wide the lens has become for modern venture capital, stretching from defense procurement and battlefield tools to space commerce and even questions about aliens. Jake Chapman leaves listeners with a strong sense that the future will belong to founders who understand both technology and the geopolitical environment their products will enter.

Test is where new military hardware goes to wait.
Mike sits down with Jenn Wilson, Head of Federal at Nominal, to talk about test and evaluation, the least glamorous gate between a program and the warfighter.
Nominal builds test data infrastructure for hardware. Founded in 2022 by Anduril, Palantir, and Lockheed Martin alumni, it reached a $1 billion valuation in March.
Jenn’s take is that acceleration comes from optimizing what you test for. Cutting test points is the wrong lever.

Test and evaluation as a mission enabler
High rate, multimodal test data
Real-time telemetry and closing the test loop

E60 – GPS-Free Navigation
How do systems operate when GPS disappears?
Mike sits down with Kara Kramer, Vice President ofRaptor Sales at Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), to discuss one of the most important challenges facing modern autonomous systems: operating when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or completely unavailable.
We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS
BONUS: Kara also shares her professional journey and how she got into the defense industry!
Whether you're building autonomous systems, working indefense technology, or simply interested in where drone technology is headed, this episode provides an inside look at one of the fastest-moving areas in aerospace.

E59 – Business Breakdown: Anduril
Anduril Industries raised $5 billion at a reported $61billion valuation—putting a nine-year-old defense tech company in the same conversation as legacy primes that have been building weapons for generations.
How did they do it, what is their strategy, and does the math make sense?
In this episode, Mike and Matthew take a deep dive inside Anduril’s products, revenue, contracts, and business strategy. They break down the Series H raise, the company’s rapid valuation climb, the difference between contract ceilings and booked revenue, and why visible federal obligations onlytell part of the story.
They also examine Anduril’s expanding product portfolio, anddebate the core question behind the company’s $61B price tag: Is Anduril the future of defense industrial production, or is the market pricing in near-flawless execution?
Topics include:
- Anduril’s $5B Series H and $61B valuation
- The gap between reported revenue and visible federalobligations
- Why Special Operations and the Border Patrol matter morethan most people realize
- The $20B Army enterprise vehicle—and why it is a rail, not acheck
- Barracuda, Fury, Arsenal-1, and hyperscale defensemanufacturing
- How Anduril compares to Lockheed, Northrop, GeneralDynamics, RTX, and Palantir
- The bull and bear case for Anduril’s long-term strategy
- What to watch next: IPO timing, task orders, deliveries, andrevenue growth
- The real bet: for Anduril to justify today’s valuation, ithas to grow from a $2B revenue company into a $20B+ revenue company very quickly.

E56 – The Fury Origin Story
This is the untold origin story of the Fury CollaborativeCombat Aircraft (CCA), as told by those who lived it.
Scott Bledsoe and Joe Murray join Mike to talk about Fury’s very beginning—way back to 2016.
Now known as Anduril’s YFQ-44, Fury originated as an SBIR project from Blue Force Technologies and may go on to become a poster child of SBIR success stories. But it’s not all good news.
The experience—and the decision to sell to Anduril—motivated Scott and Joe to start a new type of investment fund called the DoD Accelerator.
DoD Accelerator bridges the gap between venture capital and private equity, addressing the ‘funding valley of death’ they faced and the factors that led to the decision to sell their company—and Fury—to Anduril.
This is packed with never-before-revealed details and serves as the backdrop for a broader conversation about the realities of having a company in the defense industry.

E55 – Christine Fox: the REAL Charlie
There is a strange set of organizations that live betweenindustry and government called Federally Funded Research and Development Centers (FFRDCs) and University Affiliated Research Centers (UARCs).
They play an important—but largely misunderstood role—in national security.
What better way to understand it all than with a guest who’sone of the most famous pop-culture examples: Christine Fox.
She was the real person who was portrayed as ‘Charlie’,Maverick’s civilian love interest, in Top Gun! She spent 40+ years working as an analyst in UARCs and a civilian leader at the Pentagon, culminating in serving as the acting Deputy Secretary of Defense.
Today, she continues to serve as a Fellow at Johns HopkinsUniversity’s Applied Physics Lab (JHU APL), which is the nation’s largest UARC.
This interview has a ton of inside baseball that you won’t find anywhere else!

We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS

E59 – Business Breakdown: Anduril
Anduril Industries raised $5 billion at a reported $61billion valuation—putting a nine-year-old defense tech company in the same conversation as legacy primes that have been building weapons for generations.
How did they do it, what is their strategy, and does the math make sense?
In this episode, Mike and Matthew take a deep dive inside Anduril’s products, revenue, contracts, and business strategy. They also examine Anduril’s expanding product portfolio, anddebate the core question behind the company’s $61B price tag: Is Anduril the future of defense industrial production, or is the market pricing in near-flawless execution?
Topics include:
- Anduril’s $5B Series H and $61B valuation
- The gap between reported revenue and visible federalobligations

- What to watch next: IPO timing, task orders, deliveries, andrevenue growth
- The real bet: for Anduril to justify today’s valuation, ithas to grow from a $2B revenue company into a $20B+ revenue company very quickly.

DoD Accelerator bridges the gap between venture capital and private equity, addressing the ‘funding valley of death’ they faced and the factors that led to the decision to sell their company—and Fury—to Anduril.

There is a strange set of organizations that live betweenindustry and government called Federally Funded Research and Development Centers (FFRDCs) and University Affiliated Research Centers (UARCs).

What better way to understand it all than with a guest who’sone of the most famous pop-culture examples: Christine Fox.
She was the real person who was portrayed as ‘Charlie’,Maverick’s civilian love interest, in Top Gun! She spent 40+ years working as an analyst in UARCs and a civilian leader at the Pentagon, culminating in serving as the acting Deputy Secretary of Defense.
Today, she continues to serve as a Fellow at Johns HopkinsUniversity’s Applied Physics Lab (JHU APL), which is the nation’s largest UARC.

E49 – Ursa Major Solid Rocket Motors
In this episode, Mike sits down with Dan Jablonsky, CEO ofUrsa Major, to discuss solid rocket motors and how Ursa Major is doing it differently.
Once dominated by just two suppliers, America’s SRM propulsion base has been stretched thin—leaving gaps exposed by today’s conflicts.
Dan explains how Ursa Major is tackling that challenge withmodular production, 3D printing, Highly Loaded Grain propellants, and advanced manufacturing using what they’ve learned from their liquid motor product lines.

E60 – GPS-Free Navigation
How do systems operate when GPS disappears?
Mike sits down with Kara Kramer, Vice President ofRaptor Sales at Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), to discuss one of the most important challenges facing modern autonomous systems: operating when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or completely unavailable.
We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS
BONUS: Kara also shares her professional journey and how she got into the defense industry!

E59 – Business Breakdown: Anduril
Anduril Industries raised $5 billion at a reported $61billion valuation—putting a nine-year-old defense tech company in the same conversation as legacy primes that have been building weapons for generations.
How did they do it, what is their strategy, and does the math make sense?
In this episode, Mike and Matthew take a deep dive inside Anduril’s products, revenue, contracts, and business strategy. They break down the Series H raise, the company’s rapid valuation climb, the difference between contract ceilings and booked revenue, and why visible federal obligations onlytell part of the story.
They also examine Anduril’s expanding product portfolio, anddebate the core question behind the company’s $61B price tag: Is Anduril the future of defense industrial production, or is the market pricing in near-flawless execution?
Topics include:
- Anduril’s $5B Series H and $61B valuation
- The gap between reported revenue and visible federalobligations
- Why Special Operations and the Border Patrol matter morethan most people realize

- Barracuda, Fury, Arsenal-1, and hyperscale defensemanufacturing
- How Anduril compares to Lockheed, Northrop, GeneralDynamics, RTX, and Palantir
- The bull and bear case for Anduril’s long-term strategy
- What to watch next: IPO timing, task orders, deliveries, andrevenue growth
- The real bet: for Anduril to justify today’s valuation, ithas to grow from a $2B revenue company into a $20B+ revenue company very quickly.

This is the untold origin story of the Fury CollaborativeCombat Aircraft (CCA), as told by those who lived it.
Scott Bledsoe and Joe Murray join Mike to talk about Fury’s very beginning—way back to 2016.
Now known as Anduril’s YFQ-44, Fury originated as an SBIR project from Blue Force Technologies and may go on to become a poster child of SBIR success stories. But it’s not all good news.
The experience—and the decision to sell to Anduril—motivated Scott and Joe to start a new type of investment fund called the DoD Accelerator.
DoD Accelerator bridges the gap between venture capital and private equity, addressing the ‘funding valley of death’ they faced and the factors that led to the decision to sell their company—and Fury—to Anduril.
This is packed with never-before-revealed details and serves as the backdrop for a broader conversation about the realities of having a company in the defense industry.

E55 – Christine Fox: the REAL Charlie
There is a strange set of organizations that live betweenindustry and government called Federally Funded Research and Development Centers (FFRDCs) and University Affiliated Research Centers (UARCs).
They play an important—but largely misunderstood role—in national security.
What better way to understand it all than with a guest who’sone of the most famous pop-culture examples: Christine Fox.
She was the real person who was portrayed as ‘Charlie’,Maverick’s civilian love interest, in Top Gun! She spent 40+ years working as an analyst in UARCs and a civilian leader at the Pentagon, culminating in serving as the acting Deputy Secretary of Defense.
Today, she continues to serve as a Fellow at Johns HopkinsUniversity’s Applied Physics Lab (JHU APL), which is the nation’s largest UARC.
This interview has a ton of inside baseball that you won’t find anywhere else!

Test is where new military hardware goes to wait.

E60 – GPS-Free Navigation
How do systems operate when GPS disappears?
Mike sits down with Kara Kramer, Vice President ofRaptor Sales at Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), to discuss one of the most important challenges facing modern autonomous systems: operating when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or completely unavailable.
We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS
BONUS: Kara also shares her professional journey and how she got into the defense industry!
Whether you're building autonomous systems, working indefense technology, or simply interested in where drone technology is headed, this episode provides an inside look at one of the fastest-moving areas in aerospace.

E59 – Business Breakdown: Anduril
Anduril Industries raised $5 billion at a reported $61billion valuation—putting a nine-year-old defense tech company in the same conversation as legacy primes that have been building weapons for generations.
How did they do it, what is their strategy, and does the math make sense?
In this episode, Mike and Matthew take a deep dive inside Anduril’s products, revenue, contracts, and business strategy. They break down the Series H raise, the company’s rapid valuation climb, the difference between contract ceilings and booked revenue, and why visible federal obligations onlytell part of the story.
They also examine Anduril’s expanding product portfolio, anddebate the core question behind the company’s $61B price tag: Is Anduril the future of defense industrial production, or is the market pricing in near-flawless execution?
Topics include:
- Anduril’s $5B Series H and $61B valuation
- The gap between reported revenue and visible federalobligations
- Why Special Operations and the Border Patrol matter morethan most people realize
- The $20B Army enterprise vehicle—and why it is a rail, not acheck
- Barracuda, Fury, Arsenal-1, and hyperscale defensemanufacturing
- How Anduril compares to Lockheed, Northrop, GeneralDynamics, RTX, and Palantir
- The bull and bear case for Anduril’s long-term strategy
- What to watch next: IPO timing, task orders, deliveries, andrevenue growth
- The real bet: for Anduril to justify today’s valuation, ithas to grow from a $2B revenue company into a $20B+ revenue company very quickly.

This is the untold origin story of the Fury CollaborativeCombat Aircraft (CCA), as told by those who lived it.

Now known as Anduril’s YFQ-44, Fury originated as an SBIR project from Blue Force Technologies and may go on to become a poster child of SBIR success stories. But it’s not all good news.
The experience—and the decision to sell to Anduril—motivated Scott and Joe to start a new type of investment fund called the DoD Accelerator.
DoD Accelerator bridges the gap between venture capital and private equity, addressing the ‘funding valley of death’ they faced and the factors that led to the decision to sell their company—and Fury—to Anduril.

E55 – Christine Fox: the REAL Charlie
There is a strange set of organizations that live betweenindustry and government called Federally Funded Research and Development Centers (FFRDCs) and University Affiliated Research Centers (UARCs).
They play an important—but largely misunderstood role—in national security.
What better way to understand it all than with a guest who’sone of the most famous pop-culture examples: Christine Fox.
She was the real person who was portrayed as ‘Charlie’,Maverick’s civilian love interest, in Top Gun! She spent 40+ years working as an analyst in UARCs and a civilian leader at the Pentagon, culminating in serving as the acting Deputy Secretary of Defense.
Today, she continues to serve as a Fellow at Johns HopkinsUniversity’s Applied Physics Lab (JHU APL), which is the nation’s largest UARC.

Don’t miss our newsletter!
Mike and Jake host defense industry legend Norm Augustine in
a rare interview!
He started as an aeronautical engineer in the 1950s and rose
to become the first CEO of Lockheed Martin, before leaving it all.
He lived through the 1980s defense industry heyday, wrote a
hilarious book called ‘Augustine’s Laws ’ and led the industry through a massive consolidation in the early 1990s after the infamous ‘Last Supper.’ This is a first-hand account of how it all went down—he was in the room when it happened.
Norm shares his professional experiences and some amazing personal stories—like how he almost bought Northrop Grumman. This is an interview you don’t want to miss.
If you need any more reasons to listen, his resume and achievements are so incredible they sound made up:
- Co-founded In-Q-Tel, the venture capital arm of the CIA
- Chairman of the Red Cross
- President of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics
- President of the Boy Scouts of America
- Chairman of the Aerospace Industries Association
- President and Chairman of the Association of the United States Army
- Chairman of the National Academy of Engineering
- Served 16 years on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology
- traveled to 130 countries
- holds 34 honorary degrees
- received dozens of accolades, including the Pentagon’s highest civilian decoration, the Distinguished Civilian Service Award---FIVE TIMES.

Test is where new military hardware goes to wait.
Mike sits down with Jenn Wilson, Head of Federal at Nominal, to talk about test and evaluation, the least glamorous gate between a program and the warfighter.
Nominal builds test data infrastructure for hardware. Founded in 2022 by Anduril, Palantir, and Lockheed Martin alumni, it reached a $1 billion valuation in March.
Jenn’s take is that acceleration comes from optimizing what you test for. Cutting test points is the wrong lever.

Test and evaluation as a mission enabler
High rate, multimodal test data
Real-time telemetry and closing the test loop

E60 – GPS-Free Navigation
How do systems operate when GPS disappears?
Mike sits down with Kara Kramer, Vice President ofRaptor Sales at Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), to discuss one of the most important challenges facing modern autonomous systems: operating when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or completely unavailable.
We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS
BONUS: Kara also shares her professional journey and how she got into the defense industry!
Whether you're building autonomous systems, working indefense technology, or simply interested in where drone technology is headed, this episode provides an inside look at one of the fastest-moving areas in aerospace.

E59 – Business Breakdown: Anduril
Anduril Industries raised $5 billion at a reported $61billion valuation—putting a nine-year-old defense tech company in the same conversation as legacy primes that have been building weapons for generations.
How did they do it, what is their strategy, and does the math make sense?
In this episode, Mike and Matthew take a deep dive inside Anduril’s products, revenue, contracts, and business strategy. They break down the Series H raise, the company’s rapid valuation climb, the difference between contract ceilings and booked revenue, and why visible federal obligations onlytell part of the story.
They also examine Anduril’s expanding product portfolio, anddebate the core question behind the company’s $61B price tag: Is Anduril the future of defense industrial production, or is the market pricing in near-flawless execution?
Topics include:
- Anduril’s $5B Series H and $61B valuation
- The gap between reported revenue and visible federalobligations
- Why Special Operations and the Border Patrol matter morethan most people realize
- The $20B Army enterprise vehicle—and why it is a rail, not acheck
- Barracuda, Fury, Arsenal-1, and hyperscale defensemanufacturing
- How Anduril compares to Lockheed, Northrop, GeneralDynamics, RTX, and Palantir
- The bull and bear case for Anduril’s long-term strategy
- What to watch next: IPO timing, task orders, deliveries, andrevenue growth
- The real bet: for Anduril to justify today’s valuation, ithas to grow from a $2B revenue company into a $20B+ revenue company very quickly.

There is a strange set of organizations that live betweenindustry and government called Federally Funded Research and Development Centers (FFRDCs) and University Affiliated Research Centers (UARCs).

What better way to understand it all than with a guest who’sone of the most famous pop-culture examples: Christine Fox.
She was the real person who was portrayed as ‘Charlie’,Maverick’s civilian love interest, in Top Gun! She spent 40+ years working as an analyst in UARCs and a civilian leader at the Pentagon, culminating in serving as the acting Deputy Secretary of Defense.
Today, she continues to serve as a Fellow at Johns HopkinsUniversity’s Applied Physics Lab (JHU APL), which is the nation’s largest UARC.

E37 – High Power Microwave Weapons
Don’t miss our ⁠newsletter!
Mike hosts Andy Lowery to dig deep into directed energy weapons—specifically high-power microwave (HPM) systems.
Andy is the CEO of Epirus, a venture-backed defense tech startup inverting the cost equation of drone defense and swarm protection.
We talk about the tech, how it affects electronics, and how Epirus’ flagship product—Leonidas—is designed with adaptability and scale in mind. Turns out that HPM systems share more in common with an F-35 radar and an EA-18 jammer than a kitchen appliance!
The Army is currently in a rapid buy-and-try phase of these counter-UAS (CUAS) systems and is sending them to the Middle East. The systems have a host of other applications, though—the Navy is experimenting with them to disable boat motors, and the Air Force is also interested.
This episode is a defense tech episode you don’t want to miss!

E61 – Rebuilding the Test Playbook with Nominal
Test is where new military hardware goes to wait.
Mike sits down with Jenn Wilson, Head of Federal at Nominal, to talk about test and evaluation, the least glamorous gate between a program and the warfighter.
Nominal builds test data infrastructure for hardware. Founded in 2022 by Anduril, Palantir, and Lockheed Martin alumni, it reached a $1 billion valuation in March.
Jenn’s take is that acceleration comes from optimizing what you test for. Cutting test points is the wrong lever.
Topics include:
Test and evaluation as a mission enabler
High rate, multimodal test data
Real-time telemetry and closing the test loop
DARPA CIPHER Forge and digital twins
Closing the sim to real gap
The F-35 crowdsourced flight data program
Knowledge parity between primes and government testers

E60 – GPS-Free Navigation
How do systems operate when GPS disappears?
Mike sits down with Kara Kramer, Vice President ofRaptor Sales at Vantor (formerly Maxar Intelligence), to discuss one of the most important challenges facing modern autonomous systems: operating when GPS is jammed, spoofed, or completely unavailable.
We discuss vision-based navigation (VBN), 3D geospatialintelligence, and why resilient autonomy depends on more than just the drone itself. From electronic warfare to contested operations, this conversation examines how software and spatial intelligence are enabling unmanned operations, and Vantor’s unique approach.
This isn’t just about navigation—coordinate generation and targeting elements are equally important.
Topics include:
• Vision-based navigation
• 3D geospatial intelligence
• Targeting without GPS
BONUS: Kara also shares her professional journey and how she got into the defense industry!
Whether you're building autonomous systems, working indefense technology, or simply interested in where drone technology is headed, this episode provides an inside look at one of the fastest-moving areas in aerospace.

E59 – Business Breakdown: Anduril
Anduril Industries raised $5 billion at a reported $61billion valuation—putting a nine-year-old defense tech company in the same conversation as legacy primes that have been building weapons for generations.
How did they do it, what is their strategy, and does the math make sense?
In this episode, Mike and Matthew take a deep dive inside Anduril’s products, revenue, contracts, and business strategy. They break down the Series H raise, the company’s rapid valuation climb, the difference between contract ceilings and booked revenue, and why visible federal obligations onlytell part of the story.
They also examine Anduril’s expanding product portfolio, anddebate the core question behind the company’s $61B price tag: Is Anduril the future of defense industrial production, or is the market pricing in near-flawless execution?
Topics include:
- Anduril’s $5B Series H and $61B valuation
- The gap between reported revenue and visible federalobligations
- Why Special Operations and the Border Patrol matter morethan most people realize
- The $20B Army enterprise vehicle—and why it is a rail, not acheck
- Barracuda, Fury, Arsenal-1, and hyperscale defensemanufacturing
- How Anduril compares to Lockheed, Northrop, GeneralDynamics, RTX, and Palantir
- The bull and bear case for Anduril’s long-term strategy
- What to watch next: IPO timing, task orders, deliveries, andrevenue growth
- The real bet: for Anduril to justify today’s valuation, ithas to grow from a $2B revenue company into a $20B+ revenue company very quickly.

E56 – The Fury Origin Story
This is the untold origin story of the Fury CollaborativeCombat Aircraft (CCA), as told by those who lived it.
Scott Bledsoe and Joe Murray join Mike to talk about Fury’s very beginning—way back to 2016.
Now known as Anduril’s YFQ-44, Fury originated as an SBIR project from Blue Force Technologies and may go on to become a poster child of SBIR success stories. But it’s not all good news.
The experience—and the decision to sell to Anduril—motivated Scott and Joe to start a new type of investment fund called the DoD Accelerator.
DoD Accelerator bridges the gap between venture capital and private equity, addressing the ‘funding valley of death’ they faced and the factors that led to the decision to sell their company—and Fury—to Anduril.
This is packed with never-before-revealed details and serves as the backdrop for a broader conversation about the realities of having a company in the defense industry.

E55 – Christine Fox: the REAL Charlie
There is a strange set of organizations that live betweenindustry and government called Federally Funded Research and Development Centers (FFRDCs) and University Affiliated Research Centers (UARCs).
They play an important—but largely misunderstood role—in national security.
What better way to understand it all than with a guest who’sone of the most famous pop-culture examples: Christine Fox.
She was the real person who was portrayed as ‘Charlie’,Maverick’s civilian love interest, in Top Gun! She spent 40+ years working as an analyst in UARCs and a civilian leader at the Pentagon, culminating in serving as the acting Deputy Secretary of Defense.
Today, she continues to serve as a Fellow at Johns HopkinsUniversity’s Applied Physics Lab (JHU APL), which is the nation’s largest UARC.
This interview has a ton of inside baseball that you won’t find anywhere else!
